idiom_name: version column tested through sqlite3_changes() (or a driver's affected-row count) + C11 atomic_compare_exchange for in-process tokens
implementation_notes: C has no persistence layer to lean on, so the classic structure is written by hand: keep an integer version column, read it with the row, and run UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ? on one statement, then test sqlite3_changes() (or the driver's affected-row count) - zero means the copy was stale. For a shared in-process record the same idea appears as atomic_compare_exchange_strong on an atomic_uint/atomic_uint_fast64_t: the expected operand is the token the caller read, and a failed exchange returns the current value so the caller can re-read and retry. Nothing in libc or POSIX supplies the token itself, so the hand-written form is justified wherever the store or the shared memory must expose the version explicitly.
pitfalls: sqlite3_changes() is per connection: if another thread ran a statement on the same connection, the value is unpredictable and no longer describes your UPDATE.
A version column narrower than the bound value (INT versus 64-bit) truncates silently and lets stale writes pass the predicate.
atomic_compare_exchange_weak may fail spuriously; use the _strong form or loop with a fresh expected value.
